e-7661.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)+1 & \le 0 \\ \frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2) & \le -1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2) & \le -\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)} & \le {e}^{-5/3} \\ x+2 & \le {e}^{-5/3} \\ x & \le {e}^{-5/3}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+2> 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x > -2
$$

Our solution is $x \leq e^{-5/3}-2,$ which can be expressed as $\left(-\infty, e^{-5/3}-2\right].$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x > -2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2, \infty).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
\left(-\infty, e^{-5/3}-2\right] \cap (-2, \infty) = \left(-2,e^{-5/3}-2 \right]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \in \left(-2, e^{-5/3}-2\right],$ which can also be written as $-2<  x \leq e^{-5/3}-2.$

$$

\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & \ge {e}^{-3} \\ x+1 & \ge {e}^{-3} \\ x & \ge {e}^{-3}-1 \\ x & \ge \frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}}\end{aligned}

$$
[\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}},\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )=[\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}},\infty )

content.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+12 & \ge 0 \\ 4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & \ge -12 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & \ge -3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & \ge {e}^{-3} \\ x+1 & \ge {e}^{-3} \\ x & \ge {e}^{-3}-1 \\ x & \ge \frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+1>0\,⇒\,x>-1
$$

Our solution is $x\ge \frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}},$ which can be expressed as $[\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>-1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
[\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}},\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )=[\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x\ge \frac{1-{e}^{3}}{{e}^{3}}.$

$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $4.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{{log}_{4}⁡(x+2)} & <{4}^{4} \\ x+2 & <256 \\ x & <254\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+2>0\,⇒\,x>-2
$$

Our solution is $x<254,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,254).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>-2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,254)\cap (-2,\infty )=(-2,254)
$$

decision.explanation: Exponentiating gives (x+2)e^(-5) ≥ 3x, so x+2 ≥ 3e^5x and x ≤ 2/(3e^5-1). Both logarithms require positive arguments, giving x > 0. Thus 0 < x ≤ 2/(3e^5-1).

after.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}\cdot {e}^{-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ (x+2){e}^{-5} & \ge 3x \\ x+2 & \ge 3{e}^{5}x \\ 2 & \ge (3{e}^{5}-1)x \\ \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1} & \ge x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-2 \\ 3x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >0\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}].$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-2$ and $x>0,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,\infty )$ and $(0,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]\cap (-2,\infty )\cap (0,\infty )=(0,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]

$$

decision.explanation: Exponentiating gives (x+1)e^(-4) < x-1, hence x+1 < e^4(x-1). Rearranging yields 1+e^4 < (e^4-1)x, so x > (1+e^4)/(e^4-1). This bound is greater than 1, satisfying both logarithms' domains.

We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-4} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}\cdot {e}^{-4} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)} \\ (x+1){e}^{-4} & <x-1 \\ (x+1) & <(x-1){e}^{4} \\ x+1 & <x{e}^{4}-{e}^{4} \\ 1+{e}^{4} & <x({e}^{4}-1) \\ \frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1} & <x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-1 \\ x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >1\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x>\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-1$ and $x>1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1,\infty )$ and $(1,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )\cap (1,\infty )=(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1}.$

$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-1 \\ x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >1\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x>\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-1$ and $x>1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1,\infty )$ and $(1,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )\cap (1,\infty )=(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1}.$
